title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 1.2.1 Reading: Extensive Reading

PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Reference materials are books and digital tools we use to find information, such as the dictionary and the junior encyclopaedia. In this sub-strand you will learn how words are arranged in a dictionary, how to find the spelling and meaning of words, and how to use a junior encyclopaedia to find out about a topic. The words and topics come from the theme of the family.

## Strand 1.0: The Family
Sub-strand 1.2.1: Reading: Extensive Reading
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the spelling and meaning of words from the dictionary
b) read the junior encyclopaedia to obtain information for lifelong learning
c) promote the use of reference materials to obtain information

## What this sub-strand covers
• Reference Materials

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why is it important to spell words correctly?
2. How does a dictionary help us to learn?

## Core competencies
• Learning to Learn: This is developed as the learner acquires skills necessary to properly utilise reference materials.
• Digital Literacy: This is promoted as the learner interacts with digital devices to search for meaning of words and information from the online dictionaries.

## Values
• Responsibility: This is enhanced as the learner collaborates with peers to perform various roles as they search for spelling and meaning of words.
• Integrity: This is developed as the learner focuses on specific information from relevant sites when searching on online platforms.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Citizenship: This is promoted as the learner is exposed to content on the theme of the family as a basic unit of the society.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of reading for information to their learning in Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 1.0 The Family, Sub-strand 1.2.1 Extensive Reading: Reference Materials

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Alphabetical order and how a dictionary is organised

LESSON 1: ALPHABETICAL ORDER AND HOW A DICTIONARY IS ORGANISED
============================================================

## What you will learn
• Arrange words in alphabetical order using the first, second and third letters.
• Name the parts of a dictionary entry.
• Use guide words to find a page quickly.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the spelling and meaning of words from the dictionary

## Introduction
A dictionary has thousands of words. If they were mixed up, you would need a whole day to find one word. Because the words follow the order of the alphabet, you can find any word in less than a minute.

## Notes
### Alphabetical order
The English alphabet has 26 letters: a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z. Words in a dictionary are arranged in the same order as these letters.

- Look at the first letter. aunt comes before baby because a comes before b.
- If the first letters are the same, look at the second letter. father comes before friend because a comes before r.
- If the first two letters are the same, look at the third letter. sibling comes before sister because the third letters are b and s, and b comes before s.

Example: arrange these family words: uncle, cousin, aunt, brother.
First letters: u, c, a, b. The order is aunt, brother, cousin, uncle.

### Words grouped by theme
We can also group words by topic. Family words can be put into groups: people (mother, sibling, elder), places (home, village) and activities (chores, visit). Inside each group we can still use alphabetical order.

### How a dictionary is organised
- The words are grouped under the letters A to Z.
- At the top of each page there are two guide words. The first guide word is the first word on the page and the second is the last word. If you are looking for clan and the guide words are city and class, clan is on that page because cla- comes after cit- and before clas-.
- Each word with its information is called an entry. The word itself is the headword, printed in bold.

### What an entry tells you
A typical entry gives:
- the correct spelling of the word
- how to say it (pronunciation)
- its word class, such as noun (n) or verb (v)
- its meaning or meanings
- often an example sentence

For example: sibling (noun) a brother or sister. She has three siblings.

## Key words
• alphabetical order — arranged in the order of the letters a to z
• guide words — the two words at the top of a dictionary page showing the first and last entries on that page
• entry — a word in a dictionary together with its information
• headword — the word being explained in a dictionary entry, printed in bold

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Arrange in alphabetical order: widow, orphan, elder, relative.

Working:
1. First letters: w, o, e, r.
2. In the alphabet: e, o, r, w.

Answer: elder, orphan, relative, widow

### Example 2
Arrange in alphabetical order: twin, table, tree.

Working:
1. All start with t, so look at the second letters: w, a, r.
2. a comes before r, and r comes before w.

Answer: table, tree, twin

### Example 3
The guide words on a page are home and hope. Is honey on this page?

Working:
1. home: h-o-m. honey: h-o-n. hope: h-o-p.
2. n comes after m and before p.

Answer: Yes, honey is on this page.

## Activity: Line up in alphabetical order
You will need: Cards with family words: mother, father, sibling, cousin, aunt, uncle, elder, twin, visitor, home, A print dictionary
1. Each learner in a group holds one word card.
2. Stand in a line in alphabetical order. Check the second letter when two words start with the same letter.
3. Open a dictionary and look at the guide words at the top of any page. Read them to your group.
4. Find the word cousin and read its entry aloud. Name the parts: spelling, pronunciation, word class and meaning.
5. Discuss: how are the words organised in a dictionary?

## Practice
1. Arrange in alphabetical order: love, friend, home, adopt.
2. Arrange in alphabetical order: clan, cousin, chore.
3. The guide words on a page are fame and farm. Is family on this page?
4. What are the words at the top of a dictionary page called?

## Summary
• Dictionary words follow alphabetical order; check the next letter when the first ones match.
• Guide words show the first and last word on a page.
• An entry gives spelling, pronunciation, word class and meaning.

### Answers to practice
1. adopt, friend, home, love
2. chore, clan, cousin
3. Yes. fam-i comes after fam-e and before far-m.
4. Guide words

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Finding the spelling and meaning of words

LESSON 2: FINDING THE SPELLING AND MEANING OF WORDS
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Use a print or electronic dictionary to check spelling.
• Choose the right meaning of a word for a sentence.
• Keep a list of new words from your reading.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the spelling and meaning of words from the dictionary; c) promote the use of reference materials to obtain information

## Introduction
While reading a story you meet the word ancestor and you are not sure what it means or how to spell it in your composition. A dictionary answers both questions.

## Notes
### Checking spelling
If you are not sure how a word is spelt, think of the sounds at the start of the word and look under that letter. For example, for the word nephew, you hear /n/ at the start, so look under n. You will find it spelt n-e-p-h-e-w. The letters ph make the /f/ sound here.

If you cannot find a word, try another spelling for the first sound. The /k/ sound in clan is spelt with c, but in kind it is spelt with k.

Some family words that learners often misspell:
- relative (not relitive)
- sibling (not sibbling)
- ancestor (not ansestor)
- adopt (not addopt)
- orphan (not orfan)

Correct spelling matters. A reader may not understand your writing, or may read a different word.

### Finding the right meaning
Many words have more than one meaning. The word home can mean the house where you live, or the place where you come from. Read all the meanings and pick the one that fits the sentence.

- We walked home after school. (the house where you live)
- Our home is in the village near the river. (the place where your family lives)

### Using an electronic dictionary
On a phone, tablet or computer, type the word in the search box of a dictionary app or website that your teacher has chosen. Check the spelling suggestion, read the meaning and press the sound button to hear how it is said. Stay on the page you were sent to and do not click on advertisements.

### A new-words list
When you read a story or a textbook, write down every unfamiliar word. Check each word in the dictionary and write its meaning next to it. Use the word in a sentence of your own so you remember it.

## Key words
• unfamiliar — not known to you
• electronic dictionary — a dictionary on a phone, tablet, computer or website
• spelling — the correct order of letters in a word

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which is the correct spelling: ansestor, ancestor or ancester?

Working:
1. Look under a, then an-c.
2. The dictionary shows a-n-c-e-s-t-o-r.

Answer: ancestor

### Example 2
In the sentence 'The elders met under a tree', which meaning of elder fits: (a) older, respected people in a community or (b) a kind of small tree?

Working:
1. The elders met, so they are people, not trees.

Answer: (a) older, respected people in a community

## Activity: Dictionary race
You will need: Print dictionaries or a digital device with a dictionary, Exercise book
1. In groups, give each member a role: finder, reader, writer and checker.
2. The teacher calls a family word such as widow, ancestor or guardian.
3. The finder looks it up, the reader reads the meaning, the writer records the spelling and meaning, and the checker makes sure it is correct.
4. Change roles after every word.
5. Read a short grade-level text, write down three unfamiliar words and check their meanings together.

## Practice
1. Correct the spelling: sibbling, orfan, relitive.
2. Under which letter would you look for the word photo?
3. Why should you write down unfamiliar words when reading?

## Summary
• A dictionary shows the correct spelling of a word.
• Choose the meaning that fits the sentence.
• Keep a list of new words and use each one in a sentence.

### Answers to practice
1. sibling, orphan, relative
2. p (the ph in photo makes the /f/ sound)
3. So that you can check their meaning in a dictionary and learn to use them.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Using a junior encyclopaedia

LESSON 3: USING A JUNIOR ENCYCLOPAEDIA
======================================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a junior encyclopaedia is and how it differs from a dictionary.
• Find information about a chosen topic using the contents, the index and headings.
• Share information found with others.

Curriculum outcomes: b) read the junior encyclopaedia to obtain information for lifelong learning; c) promote the use of reference materials to obtain information

## Introduction
A dictionary tells you what the word family means. But suppose you want to know how families in different parts of the world live, or what a family tree is. For this you need a junior encyclopaedia.

## Notes
### What is a junior encyclopaedia?
An encyclopaedia is a book, a set of books or a website with articles about many topics: animals, countries, the human body, inventions, families and much more. A junior encyclopaedia is written for children, in simple language with pictures.

### Dictionary or encyclopaedia?
- A dictionary explains words: spelling, pronunciation and meaning. It is short.
- An encyclopaedia explains topics: it gives facts, pictures and explanations in articles that can be a page or longer.

### How to find information
1. Choose your topic and a key word. For a project on grandparents, your key word could be family.
2. If the encyclopaedia has many volumes, each volume covers some letters, for example A–C or D–F. Pick the volume with the first letter of your key word.
3. Use the index at the back. It lists topics in alphabetical order with the page numbers where you can find them.
4. Read the headings and look at the pictures and captions. They show which part of the article answers your question.
5. Write short notes in your own words. Do not copy whole paragraphs.

### Using a digital encyclopaedia
With your teacher's guidance, type the key word in the search box. Read the title of each result before you open it. Stay on the pages your teacher approves and use only the information that answers your question.

### Why reference materials help us
Dictionaries and encyclopaedias help us learn on our own, at school and at home, for the rest of our lives. When you meet a new word or a new idea, you can find out about it yourself. Encourage your friends and siblings to use them too.

## Key words
• encyclopaedia — a book or website with articles about many topics
• index — an alphabetical list of topics at the back of a book, with page numbers
• volume — one book in a set of books
• reference materials — books and tools we use to look up information

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You want to find out what a family tree is. Would you use a dictionary or a junior encyclopaedia to learn how to draw one?

Working:
1. A dictionary gives only a short meaning.
2. An encyclopaedia article explains and may show a picture of a family tree.

Answer: A junior encyclopaedia

### Example 2
An encyclopaedia set has volumes A–C, D–F and G–I. Which volume has an article on grandparents?

Working:
1. grandparents begins with g.
2. g is in G–I.

Answer: The G–I volume

## Activity: Mini family research
You will need: A junior encyclopaedia (print or digital), Exercise book
1. In pairs, choose one topic related to the family, such as twins, family trees, or families of animals like elephants.
2. Use the index or the search box to find the article.
3. Read the headings and pictures first, then read the part that answers your question.
4. Write three facts in your own words.
5. Share your facts with the class and say where you found them.

## Practice
1. Give one difference between a dictionary and an encyclopaedia.
2. Where in a book would you find an alphabetical list of topics with page numbers?
3. Why should you write notes in your own words?

## Summary
• A junior encyclopaedia gives facts about topics in simple language.
• Use volumes, the index and headings to find information quickly.
• Reference materials help us keep learning all our lives.

### Answers to practice
1. A dictionary explains the meaning and spelling of words; an encyclopaedia gives facts and explanations about topics.
2. In the index, at the back of the book.
3. To show you understand the information and to avoid copying someone else's work.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 1.2.1 READING: EXTENSIVE READING
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which list is in alphabetical order?
   A. uncle, aunt, cousin
   B. aunt, cousin, uncle
   C. cousin, aunt, uncle
   D. aunt, uncle, cousin

2. Which word comes first in a dictionary?
   A. sister
   B. sibling
   C. son
   D. sing

3. Which is the correct spelling?
   A. relitive
   B. relative
   C. reletive
   D. relatev

4. What do the guide words at the top of a dictionary page show?

5. Which information is NOT usually found in a dictionary entry?
   A. Spelling
   B. Meaning
   C. Word class
   D. A long history of the topic with many pictures

6. Which reference would best tell you facts about how elephants live in families?
   A. A dictionary
   B. A junior encyclopaedia
   C. A calendar
   D. A spelling list

7. Where do you find an alphabetical list of topics and page numbers?
   A. The cover
   B. The index
   C. The title page
   D. The guide words

8. An encyclopaedia has volumes A–C, D–F, G–I and J–L. In which volume would you look up 'kinship'?

9. Give one reason why we should use reference materials.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 1.2.1 READING: EXTENSIVE READING
========================================

1. B. aunt, cousin, uncle
   a comes before c, and c comes before u.

2. B. sibling
   sib- comes before sin-, sis- and so-.

3. B. relative
   The dictionary spelling is r-e-l-a-t-i-v-e.

4. The first and the last word on that page.
   Guide words help you find the right page quickly.

5. D. A long history of the topic with many pictures
   Long articles with pictures are found in an encyclopaedia.

6. B. A junior encyclopaedia
   An encyclopaedia gives facts about topics.

7. B. The index
   The index at the back lists topics with page numbers.

8. J–L
   kinship begins with k, which is in J–L.

9. Any one: to find the correct spelling and meaning of words; to get information on our own; to keep learning.
   Reference materials help us learn by ourselves.

An encyclopaedia set has volumes A–C, D–F and G–I. Which volume has an article on grandparents?

Working:
1. grandparents begins with g.
2. g is in G–I.

Answer: The G–I volume

## Activity: Mini family research
You will need: A junior encyclopaedia (print or digital), Exercise book
1. In pairs, choose one topic related to the family, such as twins, family trees, or families of animals like elephants.
2. Use the index or the search box to find the article.
3. Read the headings and pictures first, then read the part that answers your question.
4. Write three facts in your own words.
5. Share your facts with the class and say where you found them.

## Practice
1. Give one difference between a dictionary and an encyclopaedia.
2. Where in a book would you find an alphabetical list of topics with page numbers?
3. Why should you write notes in your own words?

## Summary
• A junior encyclopaedia gives facts about topics in simple language.
• Use volumes, the index and headings to find information quickly.
• Reference materials help us keep learning all our lives.

### Answers to practice
1. A dictionary explains the meaning and spelling of words; an encyclopaedia gives facts and explanations about topics.
2. In the index, at the back of the book.
3. To show you understand the information and to avoid copying someone else's work.
